Circle breathing system = closed (or semi-closed) circuit used to delivery oxygen and anaesthetic gases, while eliminating carbon dioxide, which involves recirculation of patient’s respiratory gases 

![](/content/exams/anzca/2015/A/1/standard-image10.png){fig-alt="Circle breathing system showing inspiratory and expiratory limbs, one-way valves, absorber, fresh gas inlet, APL valve and reservoir bag"}

**Components of Circle System **

- Fresh gas inflow – provides O2 to match O2 consumption; provides gas flow to wash out expired gas 
- Inspiratory and expiratory tubing (usu. corrugated) – conducts gas flow 
- Inspiratory and expiratory unidirectional valves – ensures unidirectional flow\
  and prevents mixing of inspiratory and expiratory gases minimise rebreathing 
- Wye connector – separates inspiratory and expiratory limbs 
- Adjustable pressure limiting (APL) valve – prevents high pressures within the circuit; prevents patient subjected to high pressures 
- Reservoir bag – stores gas between respiratory cycles, provides tactile feedback of respiration, enables circuit to be manually pressurised 
- Carbon dioxide absorber – removes expired CO2 from circuit 
- Other (non-essential) components of anaesthetic circle include
  - ventilator 
  - flow meters 
  - vaporiser 
  - out of circuit sampling line + gas analyser 
  - heat and moisture exchanging filter 

**Advantages and Disadvantages **

**Advantages** 

- constant inspired concentrations 
- conserves heat and humidity 
- allows low fresh gas flow rates 
- rebreathing of anaesthetic gases reduces cost and pollution

**Disadvantages** 

- complex and prone to malfunction/leak
- increase dead space
